text: A solar equinox occurs when the Sun appears directly above the equator, rising due east and setting due west, happening twice annually around 20 March and 23 September. This event is also defined as the moment when Earth's equatorial plane passes through the center of the Sun's disk and when Earth's rotation axis is perpendicular to the Sun-Earth line, with no tilt toward or away from the Sun. Modern definitions use the Sun's ecliptic longitude, with equinoxes occurring when the apparent geocentric longitude is 0° and 180°. The term derives from Latin *aequinoctium*, meaning "equal night," as daytime and nighttime are approximately equal globally, though not exactly due to the Sun's angular size, atmospheric refraction, and rapid changes in day length near the equinoxes. A properly aligned sundial shows 12 hours of daylight. In the Northern Hemisphere, the March equinox is known as the vernal or spring equinox and marks the start of spring in many cultures, including the Assyrian, Hindu, and Persian calendars, while the September equinox is the autumnal or fall equinox marking the beginning of autumn; in the Southern Hemisphere, these names are reversed. The March equinox is called the northward equinox, as the Sun's declination crosses the celestial equator northward, and the September equinox is the southward equinox, with the declination crossing southward. Equinoxes alternate with solstices, and leap years cause slight variations in dates. Daylight increases most rapidly at the vernal equinox and decreases most rapidly at the autumnal equinox. The solar terminator is perpendicular to the equator, resulting in equal illumination of both hemispheres. For about four days, both the North and South Poles experience daylight; for example, in 2021, sunrise on the North Pole occurred on 18 March 07:09 UTC and sunset on the South Pole on 22 March 13:08 UTC, while sunrise on the South Pole was on 20 September 16:08 UTC and sunset on the North Pole on 24 September 22:30 UTC. The subsolar point is on the equator during equinoxes, crossing northward at March and southward at September. Julius Caesar set 25 March as the spring equinox in the Julian calendar in 45 BC, but due to a 11.3-minute annual drift, by 300 AD it had shifted to about 21 March and by the 1580s to 11 March. Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar to correct this, reducing leap years from every 100 years to 97 every 400 years, maintaining the vernal equinox near 21 March. Despite this, a residual variation of ±27 hours remains. The dates of equinoxes shift over the 400-year Gregorian cycle; in the 21st century, the earliest March equinox was 19 March 2096 and the latest 21 March 2003, while the earliest September equinox was 21 September 2096 and the latest 23 September 2003 (Universal Time). On equinox, the Sun's center spends roughly equal time above and below the horizon, making day and night about equal, though sunrise and sunset are defined as when the Sun's upper limb is level with the horizon, resulting in days being about 14 minutes longer than nights at the equator and longer near the poles. The real equality of day and night occurs only at latitudes far from the equator, with seasonal differences of at least 7 minutes, and happens a few days before the spring equinox and after the fall equinox in mid-latitudes. The equilux—the date when day and night are exactly equal—is a neologism from the 1980s, gaining recognition in the 21st century, and is rare due to rapid day length changes, with mid-latitude equilux occurring a few days before spring and after fall equinoxes. The March to September interval is about 186 days, and September to March is about 179 days, making the polar day at the North Pole about 7 days longer than at the South Pole. Mirror-image conjugate auroras have been observed during equinoxes. Equinoxes are sometimes considered the start of spring and autumn, with traditional harvest festivals celebrated on these dates. In Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Central Asia, Nowruz, the Persian New Year, is celebrated on the northern hemisphere's spring equinox. Religious architecture, such as Angkor Wat in Cambodia, is often aligned with equinox events. Catholic churches have traditionally oriented their buildings to the equinox, following Charles Borromeo's recommendations. Around equinoxes, geostationary satellites experience temporary disruptions due to the Sun being directly behind them, causing solar noise that degrades or disrupts signals, lasting from minutes to an hour, with larger antennas experiencing shorter outages. Satellites also face power issues during equinoxes because they pass through Earth's shadow, relying on batteries for longer durations than at other times. Equinoxes occur on any planet with a tilted axis; Saturn's equinox, when its rings are edge-on to the Sun, happens every 14.7 years and was most recently on 6 May 2025, with minimal sunlight and more planetshine than solar light. Mars's most recent equinoxes were on 12 January 2024 (northern autumn) and 26 December 2022 (northern spring).
